docs.title: reactive.lua
docs.text: A small, dependency-free reactivity system for Lua 5.4 — refs, computed values, reactive tables, watchers, the works. If you've ever used Vue 3 and thought "I wish I had this in Lua," well, here you go.

docs.title: Guide
docs.text:
Start at the top and work your way down, or jump straight to whatever you need — every chapter stands on its own once you know what a ref is.

  1. Introduction — what this is, why it exists
  2. Installation
  3. ref() and effect() — the two building blocks everything else is made of
  4. computed() — values derived from other values
  5. reactive() — whole tables, made reactive
  6. watch() and watchEffect() — reacting to change with more control

docs.title: Going deeper
docs.text:
1. The ref family — shallowRef, toRef, toRefs, proxyRefs
  2. Reactive variants — shallowReactive, readonly, shallowReadonly
  3. effectScope() — cleaning up in bulk
  4. Deep watching — the deep option, explained properly
  5. Lua stdlib interop — table.sort() and friends, plus one thing to never do
  6. Iteration details — pairs(), ipairs(), #, and what actually triggers what
  7. Tracking control — pauseTracking() and friends, for the rare case you need them
  8. Where we differ from Vue — for anyone coming from Vue with expectations

docs.text: Prefer looking things up over reading prose? The reference has every public function with its exact signature and behavior, no fluff. See the reference index for how it's organized.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
reactive.lua gives you Vue-3-style reactivity in plain Lua: values that know when they've changed, and code that automatically re-runs when the values it cares about do. No framework, no build step, no dependencies — just require("reactive") and go.

Here's the smallest possible taste of it:

local reactive = require("reactive")
local ref = reactive.ref
local computed = reactive.computed
local effect = reactive.effect

local count = ref(0)
local double = computed(function() return count.value * 2 end)

effect(function()
  print("count is now", count.value, "double is", double.value)
end)

count.value = 5  -- prints "count is now 5 double is 10", automatically

That's the whole idea. Set a value, and everything that depends on it just... updates. No manual "don't forget to call updateUI()" calls scattered through your code, no bugs from forgetting one.

docs.title: Why does this exist?
docs.text: This library started life as the foundation for an OpenComputers GUI project — a state-driven UI needs something to notice when the underlying state changes, and reactivity systems are a genuinely good answer to that problem. Rather than invent something from scratch, we borrowed the design that's already been battle-tested by millions of Vue apps.

docs.title: About the Vue connection
docs.text:
If you know Vue 3, a lot of this will feel instantly familiar — ref, computed, reactive, watch are all here, doing roughly what you'd expect. That's on purpose: reactive.lua is built on the same core ideas as Vue 3's @vue/reactivity package, and full credit goes to the Vue team for the underlying design (the dependency-tracking mechanism in particular is genuinely clever engineering).

That said, this is not a mechanical port. It's a from-scratch rewrite for a very different language: everything specific to JavaScript/the DOM (Proxy traps, Map/Set reactivity, TypeScript's type machinery, SSR handling) is gone, and a few things are deliberately simplified because Lua — and this project's actual needs — don't call for the full complexity Vue's ecosystem does. If you're coming from Vue and something behaves differently than you'd expect, check out Where we differ from Vue — we've tried to flag the interesting cases as they come up, too.

If you've never touched Vue: don't worry about any of the above, none of it is required knowledge. Just keep reading.

docs.text: reactive.lua — code, tests, and this documentation — was built by Lephro in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic). It's a decent proof that you can build genuinely solid, well-tested software this way, so we figured that was worth a mention. See NOTICE for the full credits, including the Vue.js copyright notice.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: Head to Installation to get it into your project, or jump straight to ref() and effect() if you'd rather learn by example.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Good news: there isn't much to install. reactive.lua is a plain Lua package with zero external dependencies — no LuaRocks, no build step, nothing to compile.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Lua 5.4. That's it. (If you're on an OpenComputers build, check that it's running a 5.4-based Lua — most modern ones are.)

docs.title: Getting it
docs.text:
Copy the reactive/ folder into your project, wherever your require path already looks. A typical layout:

your-project/
  reactive/          <- this whole folder, straight from the repo
    init.lua
    dep.lua
    effect.lua
    ref.lua
    reactive.lua
    watch.lua
    scope.lua
  main.lua

Then, from anywhere your-project is on the Lua path:

local reactive = require("reactive")

That single require is all you ever need — reactive/init.lua is the one public entry point, and it pulls in everything else for you. You never need to require("reactive.ref") or poke at the other files directly (unless you're doing something advanced — see reactive.internal in the reference).

docs.title: Running on OpenComputers
docs.text: If you're embedding this in an OpenComputers world: same deal, just make sure the reactive/ folder ends up somewhere your computer's filesystem/require setup can see it. Nothing OpenComputers-specific to configure beyond that — the library was written with OC's per-tick instruction budget in mind, but that only affects how the internals are written, not how you use it.

docs.title: Verifying it works
docs.text:
If you grabbed the repo (not just the reactive/ folder), it ships with a full test suite. From the repo root:

lua5.4 tests/run_all.lua

All green means you're good to go. Onward to ref() and effect()!

docs.title: ref() and effect()
docs.text: These two are the whole foundation. Everything else in this library — computed(), reactive(), watch() — is built on top of them (or is just a friendlier wrapper around the same idea). Get comfortable with these two, and the rest will feel obvious.

docs.title: ref() — a value that knows when it changes
docs.text:
A ref is a small box around a value. You read and write the value through .value:

local reactive = require("reactive")
local ref = reactive.ref

local count = ref(0)
print(count.value)   -- 0
count.value = 5
print(count.value)   -- 5

On its own, that's not very exciting — it's a fancier variable. The interesting part happens when something is watching.

docs.title: effect() — code that re-runs itself
docs.text:
effect() runs a function immediately, and then automatically re-runs it whenever any ref (or reactive value) it read the first time around changes:

local effect = reactive.effect

effect(function()
  print("count is", count.value)
end)
-- prints "count is 0" right away

count.value = 5
-- prints "count is 5", with zero extra code from you

That's the whole trick. The effect doesn't get told "hey, count changed" — it just re-runs, reads count.value again, and naturally picks up the new value. Behind the scenes, reactive.lua noticed count.value was read while the effect was running and quietly made a note: "this effect cares about this ref." Change the ref, and every effect that made that note gets re-run.

This means the dependency list isn't something you declare up front — it's discovered automatically, every run, just by looking at what got read. Read a different ref next time (behind an if, say) and the effect's dependencies update to match.

local useCount = ref(true)
local a = ref(1)
local b = ref(2)

effect(function()
  if useCount.value then
    print("a is", a.value)
  else
    print("b is", b.value)
  end
end)

b.value = 99      -- nothing happens, the effect never read b
useCount.value = false  -- effect re-runs, now reading b -- prints "b is 99"
b.value = 100     -- NOW this triggers a re-run, prints "b is 100"

docs.title: Stopping an effect
docs.text:
effect() returns a runner. Calling runner() re-runs the effect manually; runner.effect:stop() stops it from ever re-running again:

local runner = effect(function()
  print("count is", count.value)
end)

runner.effect:stop()
count.value = 42   -- nothing prints, the effect is dead

docs.title: Cleaning up after yourself
docs.text:
If your effect sets something up that needs tearing down before the next run (a timer, a subscription, whatever), register a cleanup with onEffectCleanup(). It runs right before the effect's next run, and also when the effect is stopped:

local onEffectCleanup = reactive.onEffectCleanup

effect(function()
  local id = startSomeTimer(count.value)
  onEffectCleanup(function()
    stopSomeTimer(id)
  end)
end)

docs.title: What about computed()?
docs.text: If you're about to reach for ref() + effect() to derive one value from another — say, total.value = price.value * quantity.value kept in sync by hand — stop, that's exactly what computed() is for. Keep reading.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Full signatures and edge cases: reference/ref.md, reference/effect.md.

docs.title: computed()
docs.text:
You've got a ref, and you need another value that's always "that, but derived somehow" — a total, a formatted string, a filtered list. You could keep it in sync by hand with an effect(). Please don't. That's exactly what computed() is for.

local reactive = require("reactive")
local ref = reactive.ref
local computed = reactive.computed

local price = ref(10)
local quantity = ref(3)

local total = computed(function()
  return price.value * quantity.value
end)

print(total.value)   -- 30
quantity.value = 5
print(total.value)   -- 50, automatically

total behaves just like a ref — read it via .value, use it inside an effect() or watch(), whatever you'd do with a normal ref. The only difference is you never set it directly; its value is derived.

docs.title: Lazy and cached — the two things that make it worth using
docs.text:
computed() doesn't recalculate on every read, and it doesn't recalculate the instant a dependency changes either. It's smarter than that:

  • Lazy: the getter function only runs when you actually read .value. Never read it? Never runs.
  • Cached: once computed, the result is reused for every subsequent read — until one of its dependencies actually changes. Read total.value a hundred times in a row with nothing changing in between, and the getter runs exactly once.
local calls = 0
local expensive = computed(function()
  calls = calls + 1
  return price.value * quantity.value
end)

expensive.value
expensive.value
expensive.value
print(calls)   -- 1, not 3

This is the whole reason to reach for computed() instead of just recalculating inline everywhere: you get the "always up to date" guarantee of a live calculation with the performance of a cached one.

docs.title: Chaining computeds
docs.text:
A computed() can depend on another computed(), no special handling needed — changes propagate all the way through:

local double = computed(function() return price.value * 2 end)
local quadruple = computed(function() return double.value * 2 end)

price.value = 5
print(quadruple.value)   -- 20

docs.title: Writable computeds
docs.text:
By default, writing to .value on a computed is an error — makes sense, since Lua has no way to know what you'd want that to mean. But if you give it both a getter and a setter, you get a computed you can assign to as well:

local firstName = ref("Ada")
local lastName = ref("Lovelace")

local fullName = computed({
  get = function()
    return firstName.value .. " " .. lastName.value
  end,
  set = function(newValue)
    local first, last = newValue:match("^(%S+)%s+(%S+)$")
    firstName.value = first
    lastName.value = last
  end,
})

print(fullName.value)          -- "Ada Lovelace"
fullName.value = "Grace Hopper"
print(firstName.value)         -- "Grace"

docs.title: Stopping and pausing a computed
docs.text: Sometimes you're done with a computed — or want it to just... hold still for a while — without tearing down whatever depends on it. computed() gives you two different tools for that, and they mean genuinely different things.

docs.title: :stop() — permanently freeze the value
docs.text:
:stop() cuts a computed off from its own dependencies for good. After this, .value never recalculates again — no matter what price or quantity do from here on, total.value just keeps returning whatever it last computed:

total:stop()

price.value = 999   -- total no longer cares
print(total.value)  -- still whatever it was before :stop()

Here's the part that's easy to miss: :stop() only cuts the computed's incoming connections — what it reads. Anything that depends on total (an effect(), another computed(), whatever) keeps working exactly as before, still reading a perfectly valid value. :stop() doesn't make total unusable, it just freezes it in place. Calling :stop() twice is harmless — the second call is a no-op.

docs.title: :pause() / :resume() — a temporary version
docs.text:
If you want that freeze to be temporary, use :pause() instead:

total:pause()

quantity.value = 10   -- total doesn't recompute yet
print(total.value)    -- still the old value

total:resume()
print(total.value)    -- now recomputes and reflects the change

Unlike :stop(), :pause() doesn't touch any dependency links at all — it's purely "don't recalculate for now." The very next read after :resume() picks up automatically on anything that changed in the meantime. No manual "catch up" step needed.

docs.title: When you'd actually reach for these
docs.text:
Most of the time, you won't — a computed() that's just quietly sitting there costs very little, and letting Lua's garbage collector clean it up when nothing references it anymore is usually enough. :stop()/:pause() earn their keep when a computed is shared — say, exposed as part of a returned object — and something else might still be holding a reference to it after you're done actively using it, so simply "letting go" isn't an option.

The more common way you'll actually touch this, though, is indirectly — see effectScope(), which automatically includes any computed() created inside it.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Full signature and details: reference/computed.md.

docs.title: reactive()
docs.text:
ref() is great for a single value. But most real state is a bunch of related fields living in a table — and wrapping every single one in its own ref() gets old fast. reactive() fixes that: hand it a table, get back a table that's reactive all the way through.

local reactive = require("reactive")
local makeReactive = reactive.reactive
local effect = reactive.effect

local user = makeReactive({
  name = "Ada",
  age = 30,
})

effect(function()
  print(user.name, "is", user.age)
end)
-- prints "Ada is 30"

user.age = 31
-- prints "Ada is 31", automatically

No .value anywhere — you read and write fields exactly like a normal table, and it just works. Under the hood it's still the same tracking machinery as ref(), applied per field instead of to one single value.

docs.title: Nested tables just work
docs.text:
Got a table inside your table? Also reactive, no extra step needed:

local settings = makeReactive({
  display = {
    brightness = 80,
  },
})

effect(function()
  print("brightness:", settings.display.brightness)
end)

settings.display.brightness = 50   -- triggers the effect above, as expected

This wrapping happens lazily — the first time you actually read a nested table, not upfront when you call reactive(). So wrapping a huge structure with reactive() is cheap even if you only ever touch a small corner of it.

docs.title: pairs() and # behave the way you'd hope
docs.text:
Loop over a reactive table, or take its length, and both are tracked just like reading a specific field:

local list = makeReactive({ "a", "b", "c" })

effect(function()
  print("length is", #list)
end)

table.insert(list, "d")   -- triggers, prints "length is 4"

Same story for ipairs() — loop over a reactive array with it, and an effect that does so re-runs correctly when values change, elements get appended, or the array shrinks. (There's more nuance here than you probably need right now — see Iteration details if you're curious about the fine print.)

docs.title: Escaping the proxy: toRaw()
docs.text:
Every reactive() call gives you back a proxy — the real data lives underneath it. Almost all the time you don't need to care. But sometimes you want the actual plain table — handing data off to code that doesn't expect (or doesn't want) a reactive proxy, debugging, serialization, that kind of thing. That's toRaw():

local toRaw = reactive.toRaw

local raw = toRaw(user)
-- raw is a plain table, no tracking, no proxy

docs.title: Opting out entirely: markRaw()
docs.text:
Sometimes you have a table that should never become reactive — a big third-party object, a class instance with its own internal state, something where wrapping it would be pointless or actively unhelpful. markRaw() says "hands off, forever":

local markRaw = reactive.markRaw

local thirdPartyThing = markRaw({ ... })

local state = makeReactive({
  thing = thirdPartyThing,
})

-- state.thing is the exact same table, never wrapped, even nested
-- inside a reactive() structure

docs.title: Refs inside a reactive table
docs.text:
If you stash a ref as a field's value, reading that field auto-unwraps it — you get the ref's .value directly, not the ref itself:

local ref = reactive.ref

local count = ref(0)
local state = makeReactive({ count = count })

print(state.count)   -- 0, not a ref object
state.count = 5      -- sets count.value = 5, the ref itself isn't replaced
print(count.value)   -- 5

Handy when you're assembling a table out of a mix of refs and plain values and want everything to read the same way at the call site.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Full signatures and details: reference/reactive.md.

docs.title: watch() and watchEffect()
docs.text: effect() re-runs a whole function whenever anything it reads changes. Sometimes that's exactly what you want. Other times you want something narrower: "tell me when this specific thing changes, and give me the old and new value while you're at it." That's watch().

docs.title: watchEffect() — the simple case
docs.text:
If you just want "run this again whenever its dependencies change," watchEffect() is effect() with a friendlier name and a cleanup hook built in. It figures out its own dependencies automatically, same as effect() does:

local reactive = require("reactive")
local makeReactive = reactive.reactive
local watchEffect = reactive.watchEffect

local user = makeReactive({ name = "Ada" })

watchEffect(function()
  print("hello,", user.name)
end)
-- prints "hello, Ada" right away

user.name = "Grace"
-- prints "hello, Grace"

docs.title: watch() — when you need old and new values
docs.text:
watch() is more deliberate: you give it an explicit source to watch, and it hands your callback both the new and the previous value:

local ref = reactive.ref
local watch = reactive.watch

local count = ref(0)

watch(count, function(newValue, oldValue)
  print("count went from", oldValue, "to", newValue)
end)

count.value = 5   -- prints "count went from 0 to 5"

A source can be a ref, a computed, or a getter function (handy for watching a single field off a reactive() table without pulling in the whole thing):

local settings = makeReactive({ volume = 50 })

watch(
  function() return settings.volume end,
  function(newValue, oldValue)
    print("volume:", oldValue, "->", newValue)
  end
)

docs.title: Options: immediate and once
docs.text:
watch(count, function(newValue, oldValue)
  print(newValue, oldValue)
end, { immediate = true })
-- runs right away too, with oldValue = nil the first time

once = true stops the watcher automatically after its first callback run — useful for "wait for this one specific change and then I'm done":

watch(count, function(newValue)
  print("count finally changed to", newValue)
end, { once = true })

docs.title: Cleaning up between runs
docs.text:
The callback (or watchEffect's function) gets a third argument — onCleanup — for registering something to run right before the next trigger, or when the watcher stops. Classic use case: canceling an in-flight request or timer that's about to be superseded.

watch(searchTerm, function(newValue, oldValue, onCleanup)
  local timerId = startDebounceTimer(newValue)
  onCleanup(function()
    cancelTimer(timerId)
  end)
end)

docs.title: Stopping, pausing, resuming
docs.text:
Both watch() and watchEffect() return a handle. Call it directly to stop, or use its methods for finer control:

local handle = watchEffect(function()
  print(count.value)
end)

handle:pause()    -- stops reacting, but remembers it's "just paused"
handle:resume()   -- catches up on anything it missed while paused
handle()          -- stops for good (same as handle:stop())

docs.text: This covers the everyday shape of watch(). There's a deep option for watching whole nested structures at once, which deserves its own chapter — see Deep watching once you've got the basics down.

docs.text: Full signatures and details: reference/watch.md.

docs.title: The ref family
docs.text: ref() covers the common case. But every so often you'll hit a shape of problem it's not quite built for — a value you don't want deep-wrapped, a field you want to pull out of a reactive() table without losing its reactivity, that sort of thing. This chapter is for those moments.

docs.title: shallowRef() — when deep wrapping is overkill
docs.text:
ref() automatically wraps table values in reactive(), so mutating into them is tracked. Most of the time that's exactly what you want. But sometimes you're storing something big, or something that isn't really "yours" to make reactive — a third-party object, a huge dataset you're only ever going to replace wholesale, never poke at field by field. That's shallowRef():

local reactive = require("reactive")
local shallowRef = reactive.shallowRef
local effect = reactive.effect

local bigData = shallowRef({ huge = "dataset" })

effect(function()
  print(bigData.value)
end)

bigData.value = { totally = "new dataset" }  -- triggers, as normal
bigData.value.totally = "mutated in place"   -- does NOT trigger

Replacing .value wholesale still works exactly like a normal ref. It's only mutating into the existing value that's untracked — because that value was never wrapped in reactive() to begin with. If you do need to notify subscribers after such an in-place mutation, triggerRef() (see reference/ref.md) forces it manually.

docs.title: toRef() — pulling a live link out of something
docs.text:
toRef() gives you a ref that stays linked to wherever it came from, in one of three ways depending on what you hand it:

A reactive table + a key — the most common case. You get a ref that reads and writes source[key] directly:

local makeReactive = reactive.reactive
local toRef = reactive.toRef

local state = makeReactive({ count = 0 })
local countRef = toRef(state, "count")

countRef.value = 5
print(state.count)   -- 5, they're the same underlying value

A getter function — a read-only ref that calls your function fresh every time .value is read:

local ref = reactive.ref

local celsius = ref(20)
local fahrenheit = toRef(function()
  return celsius.value * 9 / 5 + 32
end)

print(fahrenheit.value)   -- 68

Anything else — behaves just like ref().

One more nicety: pass a defaultValue as the third argument, and toRef() will hand that back for a key that doesn't exist yet — handy for optional fields you haven't set up front:

local settings = makeReactive({})
local theme = toRef(settings, "theme", "light")
print(theme.value)   -- "light", even though settings.theme is nil

docs.title: toRefs() — destructuring without losing reactivity
docs.text:
Here's a trap: if you pull fields out of a reactive() table into local variables, you lose the connection — locals are just plain values, not refs.

local state2 = makeReactive({ x = 1, y = 2 })
local x = state2.x   -- just a number, 1. Not linked to state2.x anymore.

toRefs() solves this by converting every field into its own linked ref, all at once:

local toRefs = reactive.toRefs

local refs = toRefs(state2)

effect(function()
  print(refs.x.value, refs.y.value)
end)

state2.x = 99   -- triggers the effect above, since refs.x is linked

Worth knowing: toRefs() snapshots which keys exist at the moment you call it. Adding a brand-new key to state afterward won't retroactively show up in the refs table — but every ref it already handed you keeps working correctly for as long as state exists.

docs.title: proxyRefs() — mixing refs and plain values
docs.text:
If you're writing something that returns a table mixing some ref-valued fields with some plain ones (a common shape for a "setup"-style function), proxyRefs() smooths it over: reads auto-unwrap any refs, and writes forward into an existing ref's .value instead of clobbering the ref itself.

local ref = reactive.ref
local proxyRefs = reactive.proxyRefs

local function useCounter()
  local count = ref(0)
  return proxyRefs({
    count = count,
    label = "a counter",   -- a plain value, mixed right in
  })
end

local counter = useCounter()
print(counter.count)   -- 0, not a ref object
counter.count = 5       -- forwards to count.value = 5 under the hood

docs.title: For Vue folks
docs.text: For Vue folks: toRef()'s getter-function form is intentionally simpler here than Vue's — it calls your function fresh on every read rather than wrapping it in an internal computed() for caching. In practice this rarely matters (reads inside an effect()/watch() still track correctly either way), but if your getter is expensive and read many times between actual dependency changes, know that there's no caching layer smoothing that out here.

docs.title: Reactive variants
docs.text: reactive() is deep and read-write — the sensible default for most state. But sometimes you want something narrower: only the top level tracked, or nothing writable at all. Three more constructors cover those cases.

docs.title: shallowReactive() — top level only
docs.text:
Same idea as shallowRef(), applied to a whole table: the table's own keys are tracked, but a table stored inside it is left completely alone — not wrapped, not tracked.

local reactive = require("reactive")
local shallowReactive = reactive.shallowReactive
local effect = reactive.effect

local state = shallowReactive({
  count = 0,
  nested = { value = 1 },
})

effect(function()
  print(state.count, state.nested.value)
end)

state.count = 1              -- triggers, top level is tracked
state.nested.value = 99      -- does NOT trigger, nested is untouched

Reach for this when you're deliberately managing a nested structure yourself and don't want (or need) the overhead of wrapping it too.

docs.title: readonly() — guard against accidental writes
docs.text:
readonly() gives you a deep, read-only view of a table. Reading works exactly like a normal table; writing — anywhere, including nested — raises an error immediately.

local makeReactive = reactive.reactive
local readonly = reactive.readonly

local original = makeReactive({ count = 0 })
local view = readonly(original)

print(view.count)   -- 0, reading is fine

view.count = 5       -- error! writes are rejected, loudly

This is handy for handing data to code that should only ever look, never touch — think exposing internal state to a UI layer that displays it but has no business mutating it directly.

Since a readonly() proxy can never itself be the source of a change (nothing can write through it), reading from one inside an effect() doesn't establish a dependency — there's nothing for it to ever notify you about. If the underlying data changes through some other route (say, the original reactive() proxy it was built from), that's tracked through that other reference, not through the readonly view.

docs.title: shallowReadonly() — the combination
docs.text:
Exactly what it sounds like: top-level writes are rejected, but nested tables are left fully mutable and untouched — not wrapped in readonly(), not wrapped in anything.

local shallowReadonly = reactive.shallowReadonly

local props = shallowReadonly({
  label = "Submit",
  style = { color = "blue" },
})

props.label = "Cancel"        -- error, top level is readonly
props.style.color = "red"     -- works fine, nested is untouched

A good fit for something like a "props" object: the caller shouldn't be able to swap out which values were passed in, but you don't want to pay for (or force) deep readonly-wrapping of whatever's nested inside them.

docs.title: Checking what you've got
docs.text: isReadonly() tells you if something is a readonly() or shallowReadonly() proxy specifically. The combined isShallow() (covered in reference/reactive.md) tells you if something is either shallow variant — or a shallowRef(), for that matter, since it checks both families at once.

docs.title: For Vue folks
docs.text:
For Vue folks: composing variants together doesn't work the way you might expect. In Vue, readonly(reactive(x)) gives you a real readonly wrapper around the reactive proxy, while reactive(readonly(x)) just returns the readonly proxy unchanged. Here, both directions collapse to the same simpler rule: calling any of the four constructors on something that's already some reactive-family proxy just returns that existing proxy, whichever variant you asked for. So readonly(reactive(x)) here returns the plain reactive() proxy, not a genuine readonly wrapper around it — a real behavioral difference if you're relying on that specific Vue pattern.

Also worth flagging: this library's isReactive() doesn't make Vue's own readonly-excluding distinction — it's simply true for any of the four variants. Use isReadonly() if you specifically need to know "is this readonly."

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Full signatures and details: reference/reactive.md.

docs.title: effectScope()
docs.text: Stopping one effect() or watch() at a time is fine when you've only got one. But once you've got several related effects/watchers that logically belong together — all set up for the same "thing" and all needing to go away at the same time — tracking down every runner and handle to stop them one by one gets tedious and error-prone. effectScope() fixes that: stop the scope, everything inside it stops too.

docs.title: The basic idea
docs.text:
local reactive = require("reactive")
local effectScope = reactive.effectScope
local effect = reactive.effect
local watchEffect = reactive.watchEffect

local scope = effectScope()

scope:run(function()
  effect(function()
    print("effect A")
  end)
  watchEffect(function()
    print("effect B")
  end)
end)

scope:stop()   -- both effects above are stopped, in one call

Anything created via effect(), watch(), or watchEffect() while scope:run(fn) is executing gets automatically collected by that scope. You don't have to hang on to individual runners or handles — just stop the scope.

docs.title: Cleaning up more than just effects
docs.text:
If you've got other cleanup to do — closing a file handle, canceling a subscription, whatever — that isn't itself an effect, onScopeDispose() lets you hook into the same stop() call:

local onScopeDispose = reactive.onScopeDispose

local connScope = effectScope()

connScope:run(function()
  local connection = openSomeConnection()
  onScopeDispose(function()
    connection:close()
  end)

  watchEffect(function()
    -- do something with the connection
  end)
end)

connScope:stop()   -- closes the connection AND stops the watcher above

Dispose callbacks run in reverse order (last registered, first run) — right before the scope's effects are torn down.

docs.title: A practical pattern
docs.text:
If you're building something with a lifecycle — imagine a self-contained "widget" that sets up some reactive behavior and needs to clean up completely when it's done — a scope per instance is a natural fit:

local makeReactive = reactive.reactive

local function createWidget()
  local scope = effectScope()
  local state = makeReactive({ visible = true })

  scope:run(function()
    watchEffect(function()
      print("widget visibility:", state.visible)
    end)
  end)

  return {
    state = state,
    destroy = function() scope:stop() end,
  }
end

local widget = createWidget()
widget.state.visible = false   -- watcher reacts, prints the new state
widget.destroy()                -- everything the widget set up is cleaned up

docs.title: computed() is collected too — with one twist
docs.text: Any computed() created inside scope:run() is automatically collected by the scope, same as effect()/watch()/watchEffect(). But scope:stop() treats it a little differently: effect() and watch()/watchEffect() are fully torn down and never usable again, while a computed() is only frozen — its last value stays valid and readable forever, it just stops recalculating (this is exactly computed()'s own :stop() being called on your behalf). Nothing else that depends on that computed breaks when the scope stops — it just keeps reading whatever value the computed landed on.

docs.title: Pausing and resuming a whole scope
docs.text:
Stopping is permanent. If what you actually want is to temporarily freeze everything in a scope — without losing the dependency structure, so there's nothing to rebuild afterward — scope:pause() and scope:resume() do exactly that:

local uiScope = effectScope()
local panelState = makeReactive({ items = 3 })

uiScope:run(function()
  watchEffect(function()
    print("panel has", panelState.items, "items")
  end)
end)

uiScope:pause()              -- the watcher above stops reacting
panelState.items = 10        -- no reaction, still paused

uiScope:resume()             -- picks back up, catches up on what it missed

This is the natural fit for something like a UI panel that gets hidden and shown again: pause everything in its scope when it's hidden (no point reacting to changes nobody can see), resume when it's visible again — one call each way, no rebuilding any watchers or effects from scratch.

docs.title: getCurrentScope()
docs.text: If you're writing something reusable that should register itself into whatever scope happens to be active — without that code needing to know or care which scope that is — getCurrentScope() gives you a handle to it (or nil, if nothing's currently running inside a scope:run(fn)). Most everyday code won't need this directly; it's more useful for library-style building blocks.

docs.title: For Vue folks
docs.text: For Vue folks: this is the flat case only — no scope nesting, no detached option. Creating a scope while another is already running doesn't make it a child of the outer one, and stopping the outer scope won't cascade into the inner one. computed() values are collected by a scope here, same as in Vue — but the "stop means freeze, not destroy" distinction for computed() specifically isn't a Vue concept; that part is this library's own design choice.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Full signatures and details: reference/scope.md.

docs.title: Deep watching
docs.text: By default, watch() on a reactive() table's field only notices a change to that exact field. What if you want to know about anything changing anywhere inside a structure — a nested field three levels down, a new key being added, all of it? That's what deep is for.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
Watch a reactive() table directly (not a getter pulling out one field), and it's already deep by default — no options needed:

local reactive = require("reactive")
local makeReactive = reactive.reactive
local watch = reactive.watch

local state = makeReactive({
  user = { name = "Ada", address = { city = "London" } },
})

watch(state, function()
  print("something in state changed")
end)

state.user.address.city = "Paris"   -- triggers, even though it's nested

If your source is a getter function or a ref instead, you need to opt in explicitly with deep = true:

local ref = reactive.ref

local box = ref({ value = { nested = 1 } })

watch(box, function()
  print("box changed")
end, { deep = true })

box.value.nested = 2   -- triggers, thanks to deep = true

Without deep, that same watcher would only notice box.value being replaced wholesale — not a mutation two levels in.

docs.title: Limiting how deep you go: deep = N
docs.text:
Sometimes "watch absolutely everything, forever" is more than you need — maybe you only care about one or two levels down, and want to skip triggering on deeply nested churn you don't care about. deep also accepts a number: how many levels below the root to descend into.

local nested = makeReactive({ a = { b = { c = 1 } } })

watch(nested, function()
  print("changed")
end, { deep = 1 })

nested.a.b = { c = 99 }   -- triggers (this IS one level down)
nested.a.b.c = 100        -- does NOT trigger (that's two levels down)

Here's the full picture:

deep Reads root keys Descends into level 1 Descends into level 2 Reacts to state.a.b.c = x? 0 (or false) yes no no no 1 yes yes no no (only state.a.b = x triggers) 2 yes yes yes yes true yes yes yes, unlimited yes

Even deep = 0 isn't "watch nothing" — it still reacts to the root table's own fields changing, or a new key being added at the root. It just never looks inside any of those fields' own values.

docs.title: The one gotcha: deep-watched values are always "the same object"
docs.text:
Here's something worth knowing before it surprises you: a reactive() proxy is always the exact same reference every time you read it — calling reactive() twice on the same data gives you back the identical proxy. That means when you deep-watch a reactive() value, newValue and oldValue in your callback end up being the same object:

local identityCheck = makeReactive({ count = 0 })

watch(identityCheck, function(newValue, oldValue)
  print(newValue == oldValue)   -- true! same proxy, always
end, { deep = true })

identityCheck.count = 1

This isn't a bug — there's no meaningful "snapshot of how things used to look" to hand you for a deeply-watched object, only "yes, something in here changed, and here's the (still current) object." If you need the actual old value of a specific field, watch that field directly with a getter instead of deep-watching the whole structure.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Full details, including exactly how the depth counting works: see deep in reference/watch.md.

docs.title: Lua stdlib interop
docs.text:
Good news up front: Lua's table library already plays nicely with reactive() proxies. You don't need any special wrapper functions — table.insert, table.remove, table.sort, and friends all just work, reactively, exactly like you'd hope.

local reactive = require("reactive")
local makeReactive = reactive.reactive
local effect = reactive.effect

local list = makeReactive({ 3, 1, 2 })

effect(function()
  print("list is now:", table.concat(list, ", "))
end)
-- prints "list is now: 3, 1, 2"

table.sort(list)
-- prints "list is now: 1, 2, 3"

This works because Lua's table.* functions respect a table's metamethods when reading and writing — which is exactly the mechanism reactive() proxies are built on. No special-casing needed on our end.

Specifically verified to work correctly and reactively: table.insert, table.remove, table.sort (with or without a custom comparator), table.concat (a pure read, triggers nothing — as expected), table.unpack, and table.move (correctly moving between two different reactive tables).

docs.title: Watch out for re-run storms
docs.text:
Here's the one thing worth actually knowing: a function like table.sort() does a lot of small writes internally (every swap during the sort). Each one is individually tracked and individually triggers — which is correct, but can mean way more effect re-runs than you actually wanted for what is, conceptually, one operation.

Sorting a modestly-sized reverse-ordered array can genuinely trigger a couple hundred re-runs if nothing coalesces them.

The fix is the same one that already applies to any block of several writes: wrap it in a batch.

local batchEffect = reactive.internal.effect

batchEffect.startBatch()
table.sort(myReactiveArray)
batchEffect.endBatch()

Everything inside the batch still writes and triggers exactly as before — but dependent effects only actually re-run once, after endBatch(), not once per intermediate write. This isn't specific to table.sort() either — the same trick helps any time you're about to do a bunch of individual writes to a reactive table and only care about the end result triggering a re-run, not each step along the way.

docs.title: The one thing to never do: rawset() / rawget()
docs.text:
This one's not a "gotcha," it's closer to a landmine — please actually avoid it.

-- DON'T DO THIS:
rawset(myReactiveProxy, "key", "value")

rawset()/rawget() exist specifically to bypass metamethods entirely — that's their whole purpose. On a reactive() proxy, that means the write goes straight onto the (normally empty) proxy table itself, completely skipping the tracking/triggering logic. This isn't just "untracked" — it's actively worse: from that point on, proxy.key and the real underlying data silently disagree with each other, because reads now find the value sitting directly on the proxy before they ever get to the real data underneath.

There's no way to guard against this from inside the library — rawset/rawget skip metamethods by design, so there's no hook to intercept them with. The only fix is: don't call them on a reactive()-family proxy. Ever. If you genuinely need raw, un-tracked access to the underlying table, use toRaw() first and operate on that instead.

docs.title: What about string.*, os.*, io.*?
docs.text: Not a concern. None of them mutate arbitrary Lua tables the way table.* does — string.* works on strings, os.time() only ever reads an optional table argument, and io.* doesn't deal in Lua tables as its primary data structure at all. Nothing to watch out for there.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: There's no dedicated reference file for stdlib interop — this behavior isn't something reactive.lua implements, it's a property of how Lua's own table.* functions already work against any table with metamethods. startBatch()/endBatch() are available via reactive.internal.effect for the batching pattern above.

docs.title: Iteration details
docs.text: pairs(), ipairs(), and # all work reactively on a reactive() table, as mentioned back in reactive(). This chapter is the fine print — what exactly triggers a re-run, and one genuinely useful edge case involving break.

docs.title: pairs() and #
docs.text:
Both are tracked, and both react not just to values changing but to keys being added or removed:

local reactive = require("reactive")
local makeReactive = reactive.reactive
local effect = reactive.effect

local state = makeReactive({ a = 1, b = 2 })

effect(function()
  local count = 0
  for _ in pairs(state) do count = count + 1 end
  print("key count:", count)
end)
-- prints "key count: 2"

state.c = 3
-- prints "key count: 3" -- pairs() noticed the new key

# behaves the same way — an effect reading the length re-runs when whatever affects that length changes:

local list = makeReactive({ "a", "b", "c" })

effect(function()
  print("length:", #list)
end)

table.insert(list, "d")   -- triggers, "length: 4"

docs.title: ipairs() — reactive too, and here's the fun part why
docs.text:
ipairs() reacts correctly to value changes, appends, and truncation, same as you'd expect:

local arr = makeReactive({ 10, 20, 30 })

effect(function()
  local sum = 0
  for _, v in ipairs(arr) do sum = sum + v end
  print("sum:", sum)
end)
-- prints "sum: 60"

arr[2] = 99
-- prints "sum: 139"

arr[4] = 40
-- prints "sum: 179" -- appending past the end is noticed too

arr[3] = nil
-- prints "sum: 139" -- and so is truncating

Here's the neat bit: ipairs() isn't specially instrumented at all. It works purely as a side effect of how it's implemented — ipairs() walks t[1], t[2], t[3], ... until it hits nil, and every one of those reads (including the very last one, the miss that stops the loop) goes through the same tracked read as any other table access. No dedicated logic was needed to make this work.

docs.title: The break edge case
docs.text:
Since only what actually gets read is tracked, a loop that exits early via break never establishes a dependency on the indices it never reached:

local arr2 = makeReactive({ 10, 20, 30 })
local runs = 0

effect(function()
  for i in ipairs(arr2) do
    if i == 1 then break end   -- stops after index 1
  end
  runs = runs + 1
end)

arr2[2] = 999   -- does NOT trigger -- index 2 was never actually read
print(runs)     -- still 1

This isn't a limitation to work around — it's the same "only what was read gets tracked" rule that applies everywhere else in this library, just showing up somewhere you might not have expected it. If you need a loop to always establish a dependency on every element regardless of an early exit, don't break out of it.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: pairs/ipairs/# aren't separate functions to document — they're built-in Lua operations that work correctly against whatever reactive() returns. See reference/reactive.md for reactive() itself.

docs.title: Tracking control
docs.text: Most of the time, you'll never need this chapter. effect()/watch() automatically track exactly what they read, and that's almost always exactly what you want. But every now and then, you want to read a reactive value without it becoming a dependency — this is how.

docs.title: Why you'd want this
docs.text:
Say you're inside an effect and you need to read something purely for a side purpose — logging, a debug check, a one-off decision — and you specifically don't want that read to make the effect depend on it:

local reactive = require("reactive")
local ref = reactive.ref
local effect = reactive.effect
local pauseTracking = reactive.pauseTracking
local resetTracking = reactive.resetTracking

local count = ref(0)
local debugFlag = ref(false)

effect(function()
  pauseTracking()
  if debugFlag.value then
    print("debug: count is", count.value)
  end
  resetTracking()

  print("count is", count.value)   -- this read IS tracked, as normal
end)

In that example, changing debugFlag won't re-run the effect — reading it happened while tracking was paused. Changing count still will, since that read happened outside the paused block.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• pauseTracking() and enableTracking() must always be matched with a later resetTracking() — they push onto a small internal stack, and resetTracking() pops it back to whatever state was active before. Forgetting to call resetTracking() leaves tracking in the wrong state for whatever runs afterward, so treat them as a pair, always.
  • enableTracking() is the mirror case: force tracking back on inside a block where it would otherwise be off (nesting works correctly either way, thanks to the stack).

Honestly, most code will go its entire lifetime without needing either of these. If you're not sure whether you need this, you probably don't.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Full signatures: reference/effect.md.

docs.title: Where we differ from Vue
docs.text: If you've never touched Vue, feel free to skip this chapter entirely — nothing here is required knowledge. If you have, here's the full, honest list of where reactive.lua intentionally parts ways with @vue/reactivity, and why. None of this is a bug or an oversight — every item here was a deliberate call, usually because Lua (or this project's actual needs) simply didn't call for the extra complexity.

docs.title: How does it compare to Vue's version?
docs.text:
Feature Vue 3 reactive.lua ref / computed / effect ✅ ✅ reactive / readonly / shallow* ✅ ✅ watch / watchEffect ✅ ✅ effectScope ✅ (nested) ✅ (flat only — see why) toRef / toRefs / proxyRefs ✅ ✅ Collection handlers (Map/Set/etc.) ✅ ❌ (Lua has one table type) customRef, SSR helpers ✅ ❌ (not implemented) Virtual DOM, components, templates ✅ ❌ (never will be)

The reactivity core is intentionally faithful; the framework around it is intentionally absent.

docs.title: Dropped entirely
docs.text:
• Map/Set/WeakMap/WeakSet reactivity. Lua has exactly one table type, used as both object and array — there's no separate collection type to give special treatment to. A plain Lua table is "the" reactive container, full stop.
  • Symbol-keyed internal flags, ownKeys/deleteProperty/has traps. These exist in Vue to make Object.keys(), in, and delete obj.x behave transparently through a JS Proxy. Lua's metatables don't have a direct equivalent for the last two — reads, writes, iteration, and length are all covered, but there's no hook for "someone deleted a key" or "someone checked membership" specifically.
  • Dev-only warnings. Vue often logs a console warning instead of throwing (e.g. writing to a readonly proxy). This library prefers a hard Lua error() instead — a silently-ignored write is a much worse debugging experience than a loud failure right at the call site that caused it.
  • SSR-related branches. Not applicable — there's no server-side rendering concept here.
  • TypeScript type-inference machinery (UnwrapRef and friends). Compile-time-only constructs with zero runtime behavior — nothing to port.

docs.title: Simplified
docs.text:
• watch()/watchEffect() have no scheduler. Vue's watch.ts coordinates watcher callbacks with a component's render cycle. This library has no render cycle underneath it, so callbacks just run synchronously (still subject to the same batching that everything else uses).
  • No multi-source watch() — watch({a, b}, cb) isn't supported. Call watch() once per source instead.
  • effectScope() is flat only — no nested scopes, no detached option. Every scope is independent; stopping one never cascades into another. See effectScope().
  • computed()'s scope behavior isn't a Vue concept. computed() values here are collected by an active effectScope(), matching Vue's own self-registration behavior. But what scope:stop() does with a collected computed() is this library's own invention: rather than destroying it the way effect()/watch() are destroyed, it's only frozen — its last value stays valid and readable forever for anything still depending on it. Vue's own computed values don't distinguish "stopped" from "destroyed" this way. See effectScope().
  • No real 4-way variant composition for reactive()/readonly() and friends. In Vue, readonly(reactive(x)) gives you a genuine readonly wrapper around a reactive proxy. Here, calling any variant constructor on something that's already some reactive-family proxy just returns that existing proxy unchanged, regardless of which variant you asked for — see Reactive variants.
  • isReactive() doesn't exclude readonly proxies. Vue's version specifically distinguishes "is this reactive" from "is this readonly." Here, isReactive() is simply true for any of the four variants; use isReadonly() for the finer-grained check.
  • toRef()'s getter form doesn't cache. Vue wraps a getter function in an internal computed() for caching. This library just calls the getter directly on every read — simpler, and correct for the common case, but worth knowing if your getter is expensive and read often between actual changes.

docs.title: Not built yet
docs.text: • customRef — straightforward to add if it's ever needed, just hasn't come up yet.

docs.title: What's kept faithfully
docs.text: Not everything is different, to be clear — the actual clever part of Vue's design, the linked-list dependency tracking (Dep/Link), is ported closely to the original, because it's genuinely good engineering and translates cleanly to Lua. Batching, dirty-checking, and the overall shape of how effects, refs, and computeds interact all follow the same design Vue uses. The differences above are specifically the parts that were either JS/DOM-specific, or where a simpler approach served this project just as well without giving up anything it actually needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Toy counters are nice. Toy counters don't pay the bills.

This folder contains real-world-shaped examples — small enough to read in one sitting, big enough to show why reactive.lua exists beyond "a number that goes up." Each example uses multiple parts of the library together and — more importantly — highlights what would go wrong if you tried to build the same thing without reactive tracking.

Every example is a self-contained .md file with runnable Lua 5.4 snippets. They're intended to be copied, pasted, and mutated into whatever you actually need.

docs.title: The examples
docs.text:
File Shows off 01-reactive-counter ref(), computed(), effect() — the hello world that isn't a hello world 02-shopping-cart reactive(), computed chains, writable computed 03-config-auto-reload watch() with deep, onCleanup, and lifecycle hygiene 04-game-simulation-tick effectScope() for transient subsystems, watch() for events 05-event-bus-replacement effect() + scope as a replacement for callback soup 06-lazy-derived-graph computed-on-computed chains, and why "just recompute everything" stops scaling

Start with 01. It's the shortest and sets up the mental model every other example builds on.

docs.title: A note on style
docs.text: These aren't production code. They're pedagogical code — comments are denser than you'd write in a real project, function names are longer, and every snippet is deliberately self-contained. That's the point. Steal the ideas, not the formatting.

docs.title: 01 — The Reactive Counter (That Isn't Really About Counters)
docs.text: Shows off: ref(), computed(), effect() Difficulty: ⭐ Why you'd use this: You're tired of manually calling update_ui() every time you touch a variable.

docs.title: The premise
docs.text:
You have some state. Something else cares about that state. Right now, "something else" is a print() — later it'll be a render call, a network sync, a save-file flusher, or (let's be honest) a print().

Traditional Lua:

local count = 0
local doubled = 0

local function bump()
  count = count + 1
  doubled = count * 2
  print(("count=%d doubled=%d"):format(count, doubled))
end

bump()  -- works
bump()  -- works
count = 99  -- 💥 `doubled` is now stale and nothing printed

That last line is the bug that ships. Someone, somewhere, sets count directly instead of going through bump(), and now doubled is a lie and the UI is showing numbers from a parallel universe.

docs.title: With reactive.lua
docs.text:
local reactive = require("reactive")
local ref      = reactive.ref
local computed = reactive.computed
local effect   = reactive.effect

-- A ref is just "a value that other things can watch."
local count = ref(0)

-- A computed is "a value that watches other values and caches its
-- result."
local doubled = computed(function()
  return count.value * 2
end)

-- An effect is "a function that re-runs whenever any ref or computed it
-- read has changed."
effect(function()
  print(("count=%d doubled=%d"):format(count.value, doubled.value))
end)

-- Now the only way to change `count` is to actually change it.
-- Everything downstream stays in sync. Automatically.
count.value = 1   -- prints "count=1 doubled=2"
count.value = 2   -- prints "count=2 doubled=4"
count.value = 2   -- nothing. count didn't change. Good.
count.value = 99  -- prints "count=99 doubled=198"

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
1. The effect() ran once, immediately, reading both count.value and doubled.value.
  2. When the effect read doubled.value for the first time, the computed ran its own getter, which read count.value. So the computed became a subscriber of count.
  3. When we set count.value = 1, that triggered every subscriber of count: the effect (direct subscriber) and the computed (which then invalidated doubled, which triggered the effect again through the computed's own dep).

You didn't wire any of that. The tracking machinery did.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
The classic Lua answer to this problem is:

"Just don't forget to update doubled every time you update count."

That works for six weeks. Then someone joins the team, writes a new feature, updates count in a place you never saw, and your UI is silently wrong for a month.

reactive.lua makes "forgetting" structurally impossible — because there's nothing to forget. The dependency graph re-discovers itself fresh on every run.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Change the effect to also print the number of times it's run:

local runs = 0
effect(function()
  runs = runs + 1
  print(("[run %d] count=%d doubled=%d"):format(runs, count.value, doubled.value))
end)

Note that runs is a plain Lua local, not a ref. Writing to it does not re-trigger the effect. That's important: only reactive values trigger, and only the ones the effect actually read. Plain variables stay plain.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• ref() — a reactive value with a .value field
  • computed() — lazy, cached, dependency-tracked derived values
  • effect() — re-run a function whenever its reads change

→ Next: 02-shopping-cart.md

docs.title: 02 — A Shopping Cart, or "Why Derived State Needs a Better Story"
docs.text: Shows off: reactive(), computed chains, writable computed Difficulty: ⭐⭐ Why you'd use this: You have state with multiple derived views, and recomputing them all by hand is a bug factory.

docs.title: The premise
docs.text:
A cart has items. Each item has a price and a quantity. The cart has:

  • a subtotal (sum of price * quantity)
  • a tax amount (subtotal × tax rate)
  • a total (subtotal + tax)
  • a discount (0 by default; user can set it)
  • the final charge (total − discount, floored at 0)

You want all of those to stay consistent. You want none of them to be recomputable-by-hand.

docs.title: The naive version (don't do this)
docs.text:
-- This is the "we'll just remember to call recalc()" version.
local cart = { items = {}, tax_rate = 0.2, discount = 0 }

function cart:recalc()
  local subtotal = 0
  for _, item in ipairs(self.items) do
    subtotal = subtotal + item.price * item.quantity
  end
  self.subtotal = subtotal
  self.tax      = subtotal * self.tax_rate
  self.total    = subtotal + self.tax
  self.charge   = math.max(self.total - self.discount, 0)
end

cart:recalc()  -- remember to call this
cart:recalc()  -- did we call it? did anyone call it?

Every mutation site has to remember cart:recalc(). Every read site has to trust that someone else already did. That's not a data model, that's a prayer.

docs.title: With reactive.lua
docs.text:
local reactive = require("reactive")
local _reactive = reactive.reactive
local computed  = reactive.computed
local effect    = reactive.effect

-- The raw state. Deeply reactive: nested items, nested prices, all of it.
local cart = _reactive({
  items    = {},         -- { { name = "...", price = 0, quantity = 0 } }
  tax_rate = 0.2,
  discount = 0,          -- manually-set value, not derived
})

-- Derived: subtotal. Recomputes only when items or any item field changes.
local subtotal = computed(function()
  local sum = 0
  for _, item in ipairs(cart.items) do
    sum = sum + item.price * item.quantity
  end
  return sum
end)

-- Derived: tax.
local tax = computed(function()
  return subtotal.value * cart.tax_rate
end)

-- Derived: total.
local total = computed(function()
  return subtotal.value + tax.value
end)

-- Derived: final charge, floored at 0.
local charge = computed(function()
  return math.max(total.value - cart.discount, 0)
end)

-- Writable computed: `.value = x` writes to `cart.discount` and re-runs
-- the whole derived chain.
local discount = computed({
  get = function() return cart.discount end,
  set = function(v) cart.discount = math.max(v, 0) end,
})

-- A consumer: whenever the charge changes, log it.
effect(function()
  print(("cart total: %.2f  charge: %.2f"):format(total.value, charge.value))
end)

Now the fun part:

table.insert(cart.items, { name = "book", price = 25, quantity = 2 })
-- → effect prints "cart total: 60.00  charge: 60.00"
--   (subtotal=50, tax=10, total=60, charge=60)

cart.items[1].quantity = 3
-- → effect prints "cart total: 90.00  charge: 90.00"
--   (subtotal=75, tax=15, total=90)

discount.value = 20
-- → effect prints "cart total: 90.00  charge: 70.00"

Notice what we didn't do:

  • We didn't manually invalidate subtotal, tax, total, or charge.
  • We didn't re-walk the items array in charge.
  • We didn't add a special case for discount in any of the derived computeds.

The dependency graph is:

cart.items[*].price ──┐
cart.items[*].quantity ─┴─> subtotal ─┐
                     cart.tax_rate ───┴─> tax ─┐
                                                ├─> total ─┐
                                    cart.discount ──────────┴─> charge ─> effect

Each arrow re-establishes itself fresh on every run, based on what was actually read. If you add an "if item is on sale, price is 10% off" branch to subtotal, the dependency tracking picks up the new read (whatever field held the "on sale" flag) with zero extra work.

docs.title: The writable-computed trick
docs.text:
discount is a writable computed — a bidirectional bridge. Reading .value reads cart.discount; writing .value = x writes cart.discount (through the setter, which clamps negatives). This is handy when:

  • You want to expose a property to outside code as "just a ref", but it's really backed by a field on a bigger object.
  • You want validation logic (clamping, coercion) to live at a single choke point.
  • You want to change the representation later (e.g. move discount to a separate table) without touching every consumer.

docs.title: Why this scales
docs.text:
The classic "just recompute everything" approach works up to about 200 items and 5 derived fields. Then someone adds shipping cost (another chain), tax rules per region (branching), and a coupon system that reads from six places — and suddenly you're recomputing the universe on every cart mutation.

reactive.lua caches each computed independently. Setting cart.discount does not invalidate subtotal (which doesn't read discount). It only invalidates charge. That's the whole point.

docs.title: 03 — Config Auto-Reload, or "Please Stop Restarting the Server"
docs.text: Shows off: watch() with deep, onCleanup Difficulty: ⭐⭐ Why you'd use this: You have nested config data from a file, you want to react to changes, and you're currently doing while true do ... end with a sleep(1) and hoping for the best.

docs.title: The premise
docs.text:
You have a config file (config.lua) that returns a table. It changes whenever someone on the team edits it. You want:

  • On change: rebuild the relevant subsystem (database connection, logger, feature flags).
  • On old subsystem teardown: close connections, flush buffers.
  • No polling of unrelated fields. No restarting the whole service because someone bumped a debug flag.

docs.title: The classic approach (and why it hurts)
docs.text:
-- Don't do this.
local last_mtime = 0
local last_config = load_config()

while true do
  sleep(1)
  local mtime = get_mtime("config.lua")
  if mtime ~= last_mtime then
    last_mtime = mtime
    local new_config = load_config()
    if not deep_equal(new_config, last_config) then
      apply_config(new_config)  -- 💥 but what changed? you don't know.
      last_config = new_config
    end
  end
end

You get a boolean "something changed." You don't get "the debug flag changed, but the database host didn't." So you re-open the database on every edit, including when someone fixed a typo in a comment. Have fun.

docs.title: With reactive.lua
docs.text:
local reactive = require("reactive")
local _reactive = reactive.reactive
local watch     = reactive.watch

-- Load the config once, wrap it in a reactive proxy.
local config = _reactive(load_config())

-- Watch the WHOLE thing, deeply. Whenever anything anywhere inside
-- `config` changes, this fires. `onCleanup` runs before every re-run
-- (so old subsystems get torn down before new ones spin up).
watch(config, function(new_cfg, old_cfg, onCleanup)
  -- We don't know WHICH field changed — but we don't need to. We can
  -- diff the pieces we actually care about.
  if new_cfg.database ~= old_cfg.database then
    -- Careful: `new_cfg` and `old_cfg` are the SAME reactive proxy
    -- reference (see "Deep watching" in the docs). We compare the
    -- *current* value against whatever we want to rebuild.
    print("[config] database changed — reconnecting")
    local conn = connect(new_cfg.database)
    onCleanup(function()
      print("[config] tearing down old db connection")
      conn:close()
    end)
  end

  if new_cfg.logger.level ~= old_cfg.logger.level then
    print(("[config] logger level → %s"):format(new_cfg.logger.level))
    set_log_level(new_cfg.logger.level)
  end
end, { deep = true })

-- Elsewhere, the config file is re-read and pushed into the reactive
-- table. Note we only overwrite the fields that exist in the new config;
-- the reactive proxy handles the rest.
local function reload_from_disk()
  local fresh = load_config()
  for k, v in pairs(fresh) do
    config[k] = v
  end
end

docs.title: What's actually happening
docs.text:
1. watch(config, cb, { deep = true }) sets up an effect that walks every nested table of config on every run, so any change anywhere triggers the callback.
  2. onCleanup registers a teardown that fires before the next callback run — perfect for "close the old database before opening the new one."
  3. When we mutate config.database.host = "new-host", the deep traversal notices the change and fires the callback.

docs.title: The reference-identity gotcha (important)
docs.text:
Because config is a reactive proxy, new_cfg == old_cfg always — the proxy is the same table on every read. So if new_cfg ~= old_cfg will never be true.

The idiomatic pattern is:

watch(config, function(_, _, onCleanup)
  -- Re-read the fields you care about, every time. Compare against
  -- your own remembered state if you need "did this specific field
  -- change," or just unconditionally rebuild.
  rebuild_subsystem_from_current_state(config)
  onCleanup(teardown_subsystem)
end, { deep = true })

Or, if you want per-field change detection, use a getter source:

watch(
  function() return config.database end,
  function(new_db, old_db, onCleanup)
    -- `new_db` and `old_db` are the same proxy again — but the
    -- *fact that the watcher fired* means something inside it changed.
    -- So rebuild unconditionally and let onCleanup handle teardown.
    local conn = connect(config.database)
    onCleanup(function() conn:close() end)
  end,
  { deep = true }
)

Yes, it's a little odd. It's also exactly what Vue does, and the docs explain why.

docs.title: When to reach for deep = N instead of deep = true
docs.text:
deep = true is "walk the entire config tree every time." For a small config, that's fine. For a giant one (say, a game with 5000 item definitions in a settings table), you probably want:

watch(config, cb, { deep = 2 })
-- Only descends 2 levels below `config`. So `config.database.host` is
-- watched; `config.items[5].stats.damage` is not.

The docs have the full spec on what N actually counts. Short version: N = how many levels below the root you're willing to care about.

docs.title: Why this beats a file-watcher loop
docs.text:
• You get structured change notifications, not "the file mtime changed, diff it yourself."
  • Cleanup is atomic. No "did I forget to close the last connection?" — the framework runs your cleanup before the next callback, guaranteed.
  • You can hot-patch individual fields without diffing the whole config.
  • The dependency tracking is sub-field-accurate. The watcher only fires if the watched slice of state changed; if you later narrow the source to config.logger, edits to config.database stop spamming your log callback.

docs.title: 04 — A Game Simulation Tick, or "Scoped Effects, Not Global Chaos"
docs.text: Shows off: effectScope(), effect(), watch() Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐ Why you'd use this: You have transient subsystems (a battle, a loading screen, a menu) that spin up state, react to it, and then need to stop reacting when the subsystem ends. Manual cleanup is not a strategy.

docs.title: The premise
docs.text:
You're building a small turn-based game. Each battle:

  • Has its own hp, mp, turn, status state.
  • Runs a tick() function on the game loop.
  • Has subsystems that listen for changes: an HP bar renderer, a status-effect checker, a battle log writer.
  • Should completely stop reacting when the battle ends.

Without effectScope(), you'd manually track every effect handle and stop them all. Forget one and you leak; forget the wrong one and you get a runtime error trying to render HP for a battle that ended ten minutes ago.

docs.title: With reactive.lua
docs.text:
local reactive = require("reactive")
local _reactive   = reactive.reactive
local effect      = reactive.effect
local watch       = reactive.watch
local effectScope = reactive.effectScope

local function start_battle(party, enemies)
  local scope = effectScope()

  -- All effects created inside this `run` belong to `scope`.
  scope:run(function()
    local battle = _reactive({
      party   = party,
      enemies = enemies,
      hp      = {},
      mp      = {},
      turn    = 1,
      status  = {},
    })

    -- HP bar renderer: re-runs whenever any hp value changes.
    effect(function()
      for unit, hp in pairs(battle.hp) do
        render_hp_bar(unit, hp)
      end
    end)

    -- Status effect checker: reacts to status additions/removals.
    watch(function() return battle.status end, function()
      check_death_conditions(battle)
    end, { deep = true })

    -- Battle log: only logs on turn changes.
    watch(function() return battle.turn end, function(new_turn, old_turn)
      log(("turn %d → %d"):format(old_turn or 0, new_turn))
    end)

    -- Register the tick function as an effect too. Every tick, `turn`
    -- advances, statuses tick down, and the above watchers fire
    -- automatically. No manual dispatch.
    effect(function()
      tick_cooldowns(battle, battle.turn)
      tick_statuses(battle, battle.turn)
    end)
  end)

  return {
    battle = nil,  -- set by caller
    end_battle = function()
      -- This ONE call stops every effect/watch created above.
      -- HP bars stop rendering. Status checks stop running.
      -- The log writer stops logging. No leaks, no leftovers.
      scope:stop()
    end,
  }
end

docs.title: Why effectScope is the answer
docs.text:
Effects are great. Uncontrollable effects are not. Every effect(), watch(), and watchEffect() created inside scope:run(fn) gets registered to the scope. scope:stop() iterates them all and stops each one — in the right order, with cleanup callbacks firing.

Compare to the manual version:

-- Don't do this.
local effects = {}
effects[#effects+1] = effect(render_hp_bars)
effects[#effects+1] = watch(...)
effects[#effects+1] = watch(...)
effects[#effects+1] = effect(tick)

-- Later:
for _, e in ipairs(effects) do
  e()  -- stop it
end

Every effects[#effects+1] you forget is a leak. Every scope you should have created but didn't is a latent bug.

docs.title: The turn trick
docs.text:
Note that tick_cooldowns and tick_statuses are effect bodies — they re-run whenever anything they read changes. But they read battle.turn, which only changes when the caller mutates it:

battle.turn = battle.turn + 1  -- triggers everything that reads `turn`

So the game loop just does battle.turn = battle.turn + 1 and the whole battle state machine advances. The dependency graph does the dispatch. You never write dispatch_event("TURN_CHANGED", ...).

docs.title: When to reach for scopes
docs.text:
• Transient subsystems with a clear lifecycle (battles, dialogs, loading screens, editor sessions).
  • Test fixtures — wrap each test in a scope, :stop() it in afterEach, and effects are guaranteed not to bleed between tests.
  • Plugin systems — a plugin gets its own scope; unloading the plugin stops all its reactive effects.
  • Game state that reloads — a new save file means a fresh scope, no need to track down every effect from the old one.

docs.title: What you don't get
docs.text:
Nested scopes (a scope inside a scope inside a scope) aren't implemented — the scope implementation is deliberately flat. This isn't "coming later"; it's a conscious design choice (see the design notes in effectScope() for the reasoning). If your subsystem needs nested lifecycle, model it as a tree of scopes you manage yourself:

local battle_scope    = effectScope()
local sub_scopes      = {}

local function start_phase(name)
  local s = effectScope()
  sub_scopes[name] = s
  battle_scope:run(function() s:run(function() ... end) end)
end

If you genuinely need nested scopes as a first-class feature, fork the library and add them — the internals are commented and the design is documented. Just don't expect upstream to grow them unless a concrete project requirement shows up.

docs.title: 05 — Replacing Your Event Bus, or "Just Declare What You Care About"
docs.text: Shows off: effect(), effectScope(), and why "callback soup" stops being a valid architecture at scale Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐ Why you'd use this: You've built a global event bus and now nobody knows who fires what, when, or in what order.

docs.title: The premise
docs.text:
You have three components:

  • A network layer that receives messages and updates a shared world table.
  • A renderer that draws whatever's in world.
  • A persistence layer that flushes world to disk periodically.

The event-bus approach:

-- Don't do this.
bus.on("net:message",   function(msg)    world:update(msg)       end)
bus.on("world:updated", function()       renderer:redraw()       end)
bus.on("world:updated", function()       persistence:mark_dirty() end)
bus.on("tick",          function()       persistence:maybe_flush() end)

-- ...and somewhere else:
bus.on("world:updated", function()       -- added 6 months later,
  analytics.track("world_update")        -- forgotten in the docs,
end)                                     -- fires twice because someone
                                         -- else already wired this.

Every bus.emit("world:updated") is a leap of faith. You don't know how many subscribers there are, what they do, or what order they fire in. You certainly don't know why the renderer sometimes redraws four times per frame.

docs.title: With reactive.lua
docs.text:
local reactive = require("reactive")
local _reactive = reactive.reactive
local effect    = reactive.effect
local watch     = reactive.watch

local world = _reactive({ entities = {}, tick = 0 })

-- Renderer: tracks exactly what it reads.
effect(function()
  render(world.entities, world.tick)
end)

-- Persistence: tracks the subset of `world` it cares about.
watch(
  function()
    -- Return the slice we care about. The watcher tracks this getter's reads.
    local slice = { entities = {} }
    for id, e in pairs(world.entities) do
      slice.entities[id] = { x = e.x, y = e.y, hp = e.hp }
    end
    slice.tick = world.tick
    return slice
  end,
  function(snapshot)
    queue_flush(snapshot)
  end
)

docs.title: The point
docs.text:
The renderer and the persistence layer both subscribe to world, but they subscribe to different slices of it — because they read different fields. If world.entities[id].hp changes but world.tick doesn't:

  • The renderer fires (it reads entities).
  • The persistence watcher fires (its getter reads hp).
  • If you had a "tick counter" effect that only reads world.tick, it wouldn't fire.

Compare to the event bus, where the only granularity available is "I emitted world:updated — everybody who has that string, react."

docs.title: Why this matters when you scale
docs.text:
The event bus works for five events and three subscribers. It stops working when:

  • A new subscriber needs to know what specifically changed, and the bus only broadcasts "something changed."
  • Two subscribers depend on each other's output, and the firing order becomes load-bearing (it always does, and it's never documented).
  • Someone writes bus.emit("world:updated") without actually updating world, and now every subscriber is confused.
  • Someone else writes world.x = 5 without emitting, and now half the system is stale.

reactive.lua fixes the last two by construction: changes go through the reactive proxy, or they don't count. There is no world.x = 5 that bypasses the tracking — unless you markRaw() the table, and then you've explicitly opted out.

docs.title: When to still use an event bus
docs.text:
• Cross-process events. Reactivity is single-process, in-memory. You can't ref() a network message.
  • One-shot events with no state — "user clicked the button." There's nothing to be reactive about; it's a fact, not a state change. (Or model it as click_count = ref(0) and let subscribers react to that. Both work.)
  • Broadcasting to an unbounded audience where subscriber identity doesn't matter. Reactivity tracks who read what; if you truly don't care, you're not gaining much.

For everything else — push state, not events. Let the framework figure out who cares.
