docs.title: 06 — Lazily Derived Graphs, or "Stop Recomputing the Universe"
docs.text: Shows off: computed-on-computed chains, laziness, and why "just recompute everything" stops scaling Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐ Why you'd use this: You have derived state that's expensive to compute, or that chains through several stages, and you're currently recomputing the whole thing on every read.

docs.title: The premise
docs.text:
You're building a query builder. Users pick:

  • A base table (users, orders, …).
  • A set of filters (each with a column, operator, value).
  • A set of sorts.
  • A limit.

You need:

  • The SQL SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT ... string.
  • The estimated cost of the query, computed from the plan.
  • A preview showing the first 5 rows (which requires the actual query).

Each of these is derived from the previous ones. Changing a filter invalidates the SQL, the plan, the cost, and the preview — but changing only the limit should invalidate the preview and the cost, not the WHERE clause string.

docs.title: The "just recompute" version
docs.text:
-- Don't do this.
local function get_query_string()
  return build_select(query_state)  -- walks all filters every call
end

local function get_plan()
  return analyze(get_query_string())  -- runs the analyzer every call
end

local function get_cost()
  return estimate(get_plan())  -- runs the estimator every call
end

local function get_preview()
  return execute(get_query_string(), query_state.limit)
end

-- Every render, every event, every callback:
print(get_query_string())  -- rebuilds WHERE
print(get_cost())          -- rebuilds WHERE, then analyzes, then estimates
print(get_preview())       -- rebuilds WHERE, then executes

If you have 20 filters and the analyzer does real work, that's 60 rebuilds of WHERE per render. Over a 60 fps preview, that's 3600 rebuilds per second. Of the same string. That you could have cached.

docs.title: With reactive.lua
docs.text:
local reactive = require("reactive")
local _reactive = reactive.reactive
local computed  = reactive.computed

-- The raw input. Everything else derives from this.
local query_state = _reactive({
  base_table = "users",
  filters    = {},   -- { { column="age", op=">", value=18 }, ... }
  sorts      = {},   -- { { column="name", dir="asc" }, ... }
  limit      = 10,
})

-- Derived: WHERE clause. Recomputes only when filters change.
local where_clause = computed(function()
  if #query_state.filters == 0 then return "" end
  local parts = {}
  for _, f in ipairs(query_state.filters) do
    parts[#parts+1] = ("%s %s %s"):format(f.column, f.op, tostring(f.value))
  end
  return " WHERE " .. table.concat(parts, " AND ")
end)

-- Derived: ORDER BY. Independent of WHERE — reads only `sorts`.
local order_clause = computed(function()
  if #query_state.sorts == 0 then return "" end
  local parts = {}
  for _, s in ipairs(query_state.sorts) do
    parts[#parts+1] = s.column .. " " .. s.dir
  end
  return " ORDER BY " .. table.concat(parts, ", ")
end)

-- Derived: full SELECT. Depends on WHERE and ORDER BY (and limit).
local query_string = computed(function()
  return ("SELECT * FROM %s%s%s LIMIT %d"):format(
    query_state.base_table,
    where_clause.value,
    order_clause.value,
    query_state.limit
  )
end)

-- Derived: query plan. Reads only the string (and thus, transitively,
-- everything the string depends on).
local plan = computed(function()
  return analyze(query_string.value)
end)

-- Derived: cost. Reads only the plan.
local cost = computed(function()
  return estimate(plan.value)
end)

-- Derived: preview. Reads the string and the plan — but the actual
-- execution is the expensive part.
local preview = computed(function()
  return execute(query_string.value, plan.value)
end)

docs.title: The magic: nothing is computed until you ask
docs.text:
print(cost.value)     -- runs the whole chain once
print(cost.value)     -- hits the cache, runs nothing
print(preview.value)  -- reuses `plan` and `query_string`; only runs execute()

query_state.filters[#query_state.filters+1] = { column = "active", op = "=", value = true }

print(cost.value)     -- runs analyze() and estimate() again;
                      -- reuses nothing, because `where_clause` changed,
                      -- which changed `query_string`, which changed `plan`.

Now the interesting part:

query_state.limit = 50

print(cost.value)          -- runs analyze() again — the string changed (LIMIT clause)
print(where_clause.value)  -- hits the cache! filters didn't change.

And:

query_state.sorts[1] = { column = "name", dir = "desc" }

print(where_clause.value)  -- hits the cache! sorts didn't change.
print(order_clause.value)  -- recomputes.
print(query_string.value)  -- recomputes (order clause changed).
print(cost.value)          -- recomputes (string changed, plan changed).

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Every non-trivial app has a derived-state graph, whether you acknowledge it or not. Most codebases handle it with one of:

  1. Recompute everything on every read. Fine for small data. Kills you when analyze() is a real parser, or when execute() is a real database call.
  2. Cache at the leaf functions. Works, but you'll forget an invalidation path and ship a stale-cache bug that nobody can reproduce.
  3. A bespoke dependency-tracking system. That's reactive.lua, except you'll spend two months building it, three more debugging the cyclic cases, and one more writing docs. Ask me how I know.

The graph in this example has six derived nodes and roughly eight edges. Everything is validated by the tracking machinery on every read, so you can't get a stale cache even if you tried. If you add a new derived node tomorrow, you don't have to remember to invalidate anything — it wires itself up on first read.

docs.title: The general pattern
docs.text:
Computed-on-computed is fine. The chain can be as deep as you want. Each level caches independently, and a change propagates one level down at a time — recomputation is lazy, so if you never read preview.value, none of the chain below it ever runs.

This is the computed value proposition in one sentence: "don't compute what you don't need, and don't recompute what hasn't changed." That's it. That's the whole trick.

docs.title: Reading a signature
docs.text:
reactive.toRef(source, key?, defaultValue?) -> ref
  • A ? after a parameter name means it's optional.
  • Return types are named loosely (ref, table, boolean, ...) — this is Lua, not TypeScript, so treat these as descriptions, not strict contracts.
  • self/: method calls (e.g. scope:stop()) are written with a colon, matching how you'd actually call them.

docs.title: "Deep" vs. "shallow"
docs.text:
You'll see these words a lot, so here's what they mean, once:

  • Deep means nested tables are wrapped too, all the way down — and this happens lazily, only when you actually access a nested table, not eagerly for the whole structure up front.
  • Shallow means only the top level is touched — a table value stored inside stays a plain, untracked, unwrapped table.

reactive() and readonly() are deep. shallowReactive() and shallowReadonly() are shallow. ref() is deep for table values it holds; shallowRef() is not.

docs.title: internal access
docs.text: reactive.internal exposes the lower-level pieces (Dep, Link, ReactiveEffect, the free track()/trigger() functions, and so on) for advanced use — building a new kind of reactive primitive, writing tests against internals, that sort of thing. Everyday code should never need it; if you find yourself reaching for reactive.internal to do something ordinary, there's very likely a public function that already does it.

docs.title: computed
docs.text: See computed() for an introduction with examples.

docs.title: reactive.computed(getterOrOptions)
docs.text:
reactive.computed(getterOrOptions) -> ref

Creates a lazily-evaluated, cached computed ref.

getterOrOptions is either:

  • A function function(oldValue) -> newValue — a read-only computed. Writing to .value raises an error.
  • A table { get = function() -> newValue, set = function(newValue) } — a writable computed. Reading .value calls get; writing calls set with the new value (whatever set does with it — typically updating the underlying refs it's derived from).

Returns a ref-shaped value (reactive.isRef() is true for it). Read it the same way as any other ref, via .value.

Laziness and caching: the getter runs on the first read of .value, and its result is cached. It only re-runs the next time .value is read after at least one of its dependencies has actually changed — reading .value repeatedly with nothing changed in between reuses the cached result and does not re-invoke the getter.

Dependency tracking: works exactly like inside an effect() — whatever refs/reactive properties the getter reads during its run become its tracked dependencies, re-discovered fresh on every actual recomputation. A computed can depend on other computeds; changes propagate through the whole chain correctly.

Note: the getter receives the previous cached value as its argument (oldValue) — most getters ignore it, but it's there if you need to compare against or build on the last computed result.

If created while a scope:run(fn) is active, the computed is automatically collected by that scope — see effectScope() for what that means for scope:stop() specifically.

docs.title: computed:stop()
docs.text:
computed:stop() -> nil

Permanently detaches this computed from its own dependencies. After this, .value never recomputes again, regardless of what its former dependencies do — it keeps returning whatever it last computed, forever.

Only the computed's incoming edges (what it reads) are cut. Its outgoing edge — the fact that other effects/watchers/computeds may depend on reading .value from it — is left completely untouched; anything already depending on it keeps reading a valid, unchanging value with no error and no special handling required on their part.

Idempotent — calling :stop() again on an already-stopped computed is a no-op.

docs.title: computed:pause()
docs.text:
computed:pause() -> nil

Temporarily suspends recomputation. .value keeps returning the last computed value even if a dependency changes while paused. Unlike :stop(), dependency links are left fully intact.

docs.title: computed:resume()
docs.text:
computed:resume() -> nil

Reverses :pause(). No explicit "catch-up" step is needed or performed — the next .value read after :resume() simply recomputes normally if anything changed while paused, exactly as it would have without the pause.

docs.title: effect
docs.text: See ref() and effect() for an introduction to effect, stop, and onEffectCleanup with examples. See Tracking control for an introduction to pauseTracking, enableTracking, and resetTracking (documented further down in this same file) with examples.

docs.title: reactive.effect(fn, options?)
docs.text:
reactive.effect(fn, options?) -> runner

Runs fn immediately, then re-runs it automatically whenever any ref, computed, or reactive property read during the run later changes. Dependencies are re-discovered fresh on every run — if fn reads different things on a later run (say, behind an if), the tracked dependency set updates to match.

Returns a runner: a callable value where runner() re-runs fn manually (still tracked normally), and runner.effect is the underlying effect object — use it for :stop(), :pause(), and :resume().

options (optional table):

Key Purpose scheduler A function called instead of immediately re-running fn on trigger. Receives no arguments; call runner() yourself from inside it if/when you want the actual re-run. Used internally by watch() to control when the callback fires — most everyday code won't need this. onStop Called once, when the effect is stopped via :stop().

docs.title: reactive.stop(runner)
docs.text:
reactive.stop(runner) -> nil

Stops the effect behind runner. Equivalent to runner.effect:stop(). After this, the effect never re-runs again, no matter what changes.

docs.title: reactive.onEffectCleanup(fn, failSilently?)
docs.text:
reactive.onEffectCleanup(fn, failSilently?) -> nil

Registers fn as a cleanup callback for the currently running effect. Runs right before that effect's next re-run, and also when the effect is stopped — the usual place to tear down anything the effect set up (timers, subscriptions, and the like).

Must be called from inside an actively running effect. If there is no active effect:

  • failSilently not set (or falsy): raises an error.
  • failSilently = true: silently does nothing.

docs.title: reactive.pauseTracking()
docs.text:
reactive.pauseTracking() -> nil

Temporarily turns tracking off — any reactive value read after this call, until the matching resetTracking(), does not become a dependency of the currently running effect/watcher. Pushes the previous tracking state onto an internal stack; must always be paired with a later resetTracking().

docs.title: reactive.enableTracking()
docs.text:
reactive.enableTracking() -> nil

The mirror of pauseTracking() — forces tracking back on, even inside a block where it's currently paused. Also pushes onto the same stack; also must be paired with a later resetTracking().

docs.title: reactive.resetTracking()
docs.text:
reactive.resetTracking() -> nil

Restores tracking to whatever state was active before the most recent unmatched pauseTracking()/enableTracking() call (pops the stack pushed by either of those). Calling it with nothing on the stack resets tracking to "on."

These three are available directly at the top level (reactive.pauseTracking() and so on) — see Tracking control for when you'd actually want to use them (rarely).

docs.title: reactive
docs.text: See reactive() for an introduction to reactive, isReactive, isProxy, toRaw, markRaw, and toReactive with examples. See Reactive variants for an introduction to shallowReactive, readonly, and shallowReadonly (documented further down in this same file) with examples.

docs.title: reactive.reactive(target)
docs.text:
reactive.reactive(target) -> table

Wraps target (a plain Lua table) in a reactive, deep, read/write proxy. Reads and writes go through normal table syntax (proxy.key, proxy.key = value) — no .value involved.

  • If target isn't a table, it's returned unchanged.
  • If target is already a proxy from any of the four reactive-family constructors (reactive, shallowReactive, readonly, shallowReadonly), it's returned unchanged.
  • If target was marked with markRaw(), it's returned unchanged.
  • Calling reactive() twice on the same raw table returns the exact same proxy both times — there's no risk of ending up with two different proxies over the same data.
  • Nested table values are wrapped the same way (as reactive()), lazily — only when actually read, not upfront.
  • A ref stored as a field's value auto-unwraps on read, and a write to that field forwards into the ref's .value instead of replacing the ref itself. See reactive().
  • pairs(), #, and ipairs() all work and are reactive. See Iteration details for exactly what triggers what.

docs.title: reactive.shallowReactive(target)
docs.text:
reactive.shallowReactive(target) -> table

Like reactive(), but only the top-level table's own keys are tracked and lazily wrapped — a table value stored at a key is returned exactly as-is, not wrapped in anything.

docs.title: reactive.readonly(target)
docs.text:
reactive.readonly(target) -> table

Wraps target in a deep, read-only proxy. Reading works normally; writing anywhere — including into nested tables, which are themselves wrapped as readonly() too — raises an error immediately.

Reading through a readonly() proxy does not track a dependency: a readonly proxy can never itself be the source of a change, so there's nothing meaningful to track.

docs.title: reactive.shallowReadonly(target)
docs.text:
reactive.shallowReadonly(target) -> table

Combines readonly() and shallowReactive(): top-level writes error, but a table value stored at a key is left exactly as given — not wrapped in reactive(), not wrapped in readonly(), fully mutable and untracked.

docs.title: reactive.isReactive(value)
docs.text:
reactive.isReactive(value) -> boolean

True for a proxy produced by any of the four variant constructors (reactive, shallowReactive, readonly, shallowReadonly). False for a plain table, nil, or anything else.

Note: unlike Vue's own isReactive(), this does not exclude a pure readonly() proxy — it's true for any of the four variants. Use isReadonly() below if you need to know specifically whether something is readonly.

docs.title: reactive.isReadonly(value)
docs.text:
reactive.isReadonly(value) -> boolean

True specifically for a readonly() or shallowReadonly() proxy. False for a plain reactive()/shallowReactive() proxy, a plain table, or anything else.

docs.title: reactive.isShallow(value)
docs.text:
reactive.isShallow(value) -> boolean

True specifically for a shallowReactive() or shallowReadonly() proxy. False for a plain reactive()/readonly() proxy or anything else.

This is reactive.lua's own isShallow(), checking a reactive-family proxy specifically. There's also a combined top-level reactive.isShallow() (exposed from init.lua) that additionally recognizes a shallowRef() — see reference/ref.md for that side of it. The two checks look at structurally different shapes, so trying one after the other is safe: nothing is ever both a ref and a reactive-family proxy at once.

docs.title: reactive.isProxy(value)
docs.text:
reactive.isProxy(value) -> boolean

Same check as isReactive() — an alias, kept as a separate name to match Vue's own API surface.

docs.title: reactive.toRaw(value)
docs.text:
reactive.toRaw(value) -> any

Returns the underlying raw table of a reactive-family proxy (any variant). If value isn't a proxy, returns it unchanged — safe to call on anything, proxy or not.

docs.title: reactive.markRaw(value)
docs.text:
reactive.markRaw(value) -> value

Marks value so none of the four reactive-family constructors ever wrap it, even nested inside a reactive() structure. Returns value itself, so it's safe to use inline:

local state = reactive.reactive({
  thing = reactive.markRaw(someTable),
})

Only affects tables — calling it on a non-table value is a harmless no-op that just returns the value back.

docs.title: reactive.toReactive(value)
docs.text:
reactive.toReactive(value) -> any

reactive(value) if value is a table, otherwise value unchanged. A small convenience mostly useful when writing your own code that wants "wrap it if it's wrappable, leave it alone otherwise" without an extra type() check at every call site.

docs.title: ref
docs.text: See ref() and effect() for an introduction to ref, isRef, unref, toValue, and triggerRef with examples. See The ref family for an introduction to shallowRef, toRef, toRefs, and proxyRefs (documented further down in this same file) with examples.

docs.title: reactive.ref(value)
docs.text:
reactive.ref(value) -> ref

Wraps value in a ref. Access/change the value via .value.

  • If value is already a ref (of any kind — ref, shallowRef, computed, or either shape toRef() returns), returns it unchanged.
  • If value is a table, it's deep-wrapped via reactive() — mutating a nested field of .value is tracked/triggers just like mutating the ref itself. See reference/reactive.md for what "deep" means exactly.
  • Reading .value inside an effect() or watch() tracks it. Writing a new value (compared by toRaw() on both sides, so a reactive proxy and its own underlying raw table count as equal) triggers subscribers if the value actually changed.

docs.title: reactive.isRef(value)
docs.text:
reactive.isRef(value) -> boolean

True for anything produced by ref(), shallowRef(), computed(), or toRef() (either of its two return shapes). False for anything else, including plain tables and nil — safe to call on anything.

docs.title: reactive.unref(value)
docs.text:
reactive.unref(value) -> any

Returns value.value if value is a ref, otherwise returns value unchanged. Handy when a function accepts "a ref or a plain value" and just wants the current value either way.

docs.title: reactive.toValue(source)
docs.text:
reactive.toValue(source) -> any

Like unref(), but also calls through a zero-argument getter function:

local reactive = require("reactive")
local toValue = reactive.toValue

toValue(reactive.ref(5))         -- 5
toValue(5)                       -- 5
toValue(function() return 5 end) -- 5

docs.title: reactive.triggerRef(ref)
docs.text:
reactive.triggerRef(ref) -> nil

Force-notifies a ref's subscribers even if .value itself didn't change by comparison. Useful after mutating a table stored inside a shallow ref in place — since a shallow ref's stored table is never wrapped, mutating into it produces no tracking/triggering on its own:

local shallowRef = reactive.shallowRef
local effect = reactive.effect
local triggerRef = reactive.triggerRef

local state = shallowRef({ count = 0 })

effect(function()
  print(state.value.count)
end)

state.value.count = 1   -- nothing happens, this write isn't tracked
triggerRef(state)       -- forces the effect above to re-run

For a normal (non-shallow) ref(), you won't usually need this — nested mutations are already tracked because the table is deep-wrapped automatically.

docs.title: reactive.shallowRef(value)
docs.text:
reactive.shallowRef(value) -> ref

Like ref(), but a table value is stored exactly as given — not deep-wrapped via reactive(). Reassigning .value wholesale still tracks/triggers normally (compared via toRaw() on both sides, same as ref()). Mutating into the stored value in place is not tracked — use triggerRef() to notify manually after doing so.

docs.title: reactive.isShallow(value)
docs.text:
reactive.isShallow(value) -> boolean

True only for a ref created by shallowRef() specifically — false for a normal ref(), a computed(), either shape toRef() returns, or any non-ref value.

(This is ref.lua's own isShallow(). There's also a combined top-level reactive.isShallow() that additionally recognizes shallowReactive()/shallowReadonly() proxies — see reference/reactive.md — the one described here is what that combined version delegates to for the ref case.)

docs.title: reactive.toRef(source, key?, defaultValue?)
docs.text:
reactive.toRef(source, key?, defaultValue?) -> ref

Returns a ref, with the exact behavior depending on what's passed — checked in this order:

  1. source is already a ref (any kind) — returned unchanged.
  2. source is a function — wrapped in a read-only ref whose .value calls the function fresh on every read. Writing .value errors, same as a getter-only computed(). (See the "For Vue folks" note in The ref family — this doesn't cache internally the way Vue's own getter-ref does.)
  3. source is a table and key is given — a ref with no value of its own: reading/writing .value reads/writes source[key] directly. If source is a reactive() proxy, tracking/triggering comes entirely from source's own reactivity — this ref adds none of its own. If source[key] is currently nil, .value returns defaultValue instead.
  4. Anything else — same as reactive.ref(source).

If the value already at source[key] (case 3) is itself a ref, toRef() returns that existing ref as-is rather than wrapping it in another layer.

docs.title: reactive.toRefs(source)
docs.text:
reactive.toRefs(source) -> table

Converts a reactive() table into a plain Lua table of refs, one per key present at call time — built by calling toRef(source, key) for each. Not itself reactive to keys added to source later (the key set is a one-time snapshot), but every ref it returns stays correctly linked to its own key going forward.

docs.title: reactive.proxyRefs(objectWithRefs)
docs.text:
reactive.proxyRefs(objectWithRefs) -> table

Wraps a plain table so that reads auto-unwrap any ref-valued fields, and writes to a field currently holding a ref forward into that ref's .value instead of replacing the ref itself. Fields holding plain (non-ref) values pass through untouched in both directions.

If objectWithRefs is already a reactive() proxy, this is a no-op that returns it unchanged — a reactive() proxy already auto-unwraps refs on its own.

docs.title: scope
docs.text: See effectScope() for an introduction with examples.

docs.title: reactive.effectScope()
docs.text:
reactive.effectScope() -> EffectScope

Creates a new scope, starting active.

docs.title: scope:run(fn)
docs.text:
scope:run(fn) -> any

Runs fn() with this scope active. Any effect(), watch(), watchEffect(), or computed() created during fn is collected by this scope.

Returns whatever fn returns. If the scope was already stopped, fn is not called at all and this returns nil.

docs.title: scope:stop()
docs.text:
scope:stop() -> nil

Stops every effect/watcher this scope collected, then runs every onScopeDispose() callback registered against it, in reverse registration order (last in, first run). Marks the scope inactive.

computed() is handled differently from the rest: effect() and watch()/watchEffect() are fully torn down and never usable again. A collected computed() is only frozen — equivalent to calling its own :stop() — so its last value stays valid and readable forever for anything still depending on it; it just never recomputes again.

Idempotent — calling :stop() again on an already-stopped scope does nothing.

docs.title: scope:pause()
docs.text:
scope:pause() -> nil

Calls :pause() on every effect/watcher/computed this scope has collected. A no-op if the scope is already stopped.

docs.title: scope:resume()
docs.text:
scope:resume() -> nil

Calls :resume() on every effect/watcher/computed this scope has collected. A no-op if the scope is already stopped.

docs.title: scope.active
docs.text:
scope.active -> boolean

Plain boolean field. true until :stop() is called.

docs.title: reactive.getCurrentScope()
docs.text:
reactive.getCurrentScope() -> EffectScope | nil

Returns whichever scope is currently running (i.e. the innermost active scope:run(fn) call), or nil if none is active.

docs.title: reactive.onScopeDispose(fn, failSilently?)
docs.text:
reactive.onScopeDispose(fn, failSilently?) -> nil

Registers fn to run when the currently active scope is stopped — must be called from within a scope:run(fn) call.

  • failSilently not set (or falsy): raises an error if there's no active scope.
  • failSilently = true: silently does nothing instead.

docs.title: watch
docs.text: See watch() and watchEffect() for an introduction with examples. See Deep watching for the full deep option detail, documented further down in this same file.

docs.title: reactive.watch(source, cb, options?)
docs.text:
reactive.watch(source, cb, options?) -> WatchHandle

Watches source and calls cb(newValue, oldValue, onCleanup) when it changes.

source can be:

  • a ref (or computed)
  • a reactive() table
  • a zero-argument getter function

Not supported: multiple sources in one call (no watch({a, b}, cb) form) — call watch() once per source instead.

cb(newValue, oldValue, onCleanup):

  • oldValue is nil on the very first call if options.immediate is set. On every subsequent call, it's the actual previous value.
  • onCleanup(fn) registers fn to run right before the next time cb fires, or when the watcher is stopped.

options (optional table):

Key Effect immediate Run cb once immediately, in addition to on future changes. oldValue is nil on that first call. once Automatically stop the watcher after cb's first run. deep Watch nested changes too, not just the top-level value. true/false, or a non-negative integer for a depth limit. See "The deep option" below and Deep watching.

Returns a WatchHandle: callable directly to stop (handle()), plus explicit methods:

Method Effect handle:stop() Same as calling handle() — stops the watcher for good. handle:pause() Temporarily stops reacting to changes. handle:resume() Resumes; catches up on anything that changed while paused.

docs.title: The deep option, precisely
docs.text:
• deep omitted, source is a reactive() table: fully unlimited depth. (This is the "deep by default" behavior — no options needed.)
  • deep omitted, source is anything else (ref, computed, getter): no descent at all — only the top-level value itself is compared.
  • deep = true: unlimited depth, regardless of source type.
  • deep = false: same as omitting it for a non-reactive() source (no descent). For a reactive() source, this narrows the otherwise-implicit unlimited depth down to root-level only — equivalent to deep = 0.
  • deep = N (a non-negative integer): descends N levels below the root. N = 0 still reads (and reacts to changes on) the root value's own keys — it just never looks inside any of those keys' own values. A negative number raises an error immediately.

Reference-identity note: when deep tracking is active and the value returned is itself a reactive() proxy, cb's newValue and oldValue are the same object reference (a reactive() proxy is always the same reference across reads) — the fact that the watcher fired at all is the signal that something changed, not a reference comparison. See Deep watching for the full explanation with an example.

docs.title: reactive.watchEffect(fn, options?)
docs.text:
reactive.watchEffect(fn, options?) -> WatchHandle

Runs fn(onCleanup) immediately and re-runs it whenever anything it reads (refs, computed values, or reactive() properties) later changes. Unlike watch(), there's no separate source — whatever fn reads is what gets tracked, discovered fresh on every run, same as effect().

options (optional table):

Key Effect once Automatically stop after the first run's dependencies trigger a re-run once. (There's no immediate option here — watchEffect() is always immediate by definition.)

Returns the same kind of WatchHandle as watch().

docs.title: reactive.onWatcherCleanup(fn, failSilently?)
docs.text:
reactive.onWatcherCleanup(fn, failSilently?) -> nil

The free-function form of registering a cleanup — normally you'd use the onCleanup parameter passed into cb/fn instead, but this is available directly if needed. Must be called while a watcher is actively running.

  • failSilently not set (or falsy): raises an error if there's no active watcher.
  • failSilently = true: silently does nothing instead.
